subject.title: Houses on the Shore of Lake Cernica
subject.author: Francisc Sirato

title: Two Wikipedias Can't Agree What Nationality Painted This
standfirst: Francisc Șirato founded an artists' group with no manifesto, catalogued Romania's peasant textiles, and painted the same Black Sea coast every painter of his generation painted. English and Romanian Wikipedia can't agree what he was — a Hungarian craftsman's son, or the descendant of a French village Vienna built from a blueprint.

sections.heading: A Well-Digger's Grandson in a Neighbourhood Named for Its Own Poverty
sections.body:
Șirato's grandfather was a fântânar — a well-digger — who moved to Craiova before the 1859 union of the Romanian principalities. His father worked in construction and raised the family in Dănești, a neighbourhood on the city's edge. He wanted the boy in a commercial school, training for a ledger; the boy kept wandering instead to the lithography workshop at Craiova's Graphic Institute, and by around 1897 had learned the trade well enough to design what accounts of his life call Romania's first colour poster, for Traian Demetrescu's novel *Cum iubim* — a job that reportedly paid him 120 lei, a serious sum for an apprentice at the time.

Right there the record splits. Romanian Wikipedia says the well-digger's family were French peasants, colonised in Banat at the end of the eighteenth century. English Wikipedia calls them an ethnic Hungarian family of craftsmen, and gives his name in its Hungarian form: Sirató Ferenc. Neither article shows any sign of having read the other.

sections.heading: The Village Vienna Laid Out Like a Chessboard
sections.body:
If the French version is right, it points to a specific, strange piece of imperial planning. In 1770 and 1771, Empress Maria Theresa's administration resettled the depopulated Banat with Catholics only, sending south-German colonists — later known as the Banat Swabians — alongside French settlers from Lorraine and Alsace into three purpose-built villages: Saint-Hubert, Charleville and Seultour, laid out on a grid, their streets meeting at right angles like fields ruled off on paper. French held on there into the second half of the nineteenth century before German displaced it and the colonists were absorbed into the surrounding Swabian population.

A family that left one of those villages for Craiova, on this account, would have carried a vanishing French-Habsburg enclave a full century after Vienna had drawn it into existence.

sections.heading: Düsseldorf Without the Money for the Academy
sections.body: In 1898 Șirato travelled to Düsseldorf meaning to study painting and found he couldn't afford the tuition; he spent the year working as an engraving apprentice instead and came home in 1899 to enrol at Bucharest's National School of Fine Arts. He drew for the satirical magazines *Furnica*, *Paravanul* and *Cronica*, some of the work tied to the 1907 peasant uprising, and first showed at the Official Salon that same year. Between 1908 and 1914, exhibiting with the Tinerimea artistică group, he was working in pointillism and colour division, then pulling toward the more architectural, balanced structure he found in Cézanne — a technical apprenticeship that ran almost twenty years longer than his formal one.

sections.heading: Four Names and No Programme
sections.body: The group that made Șirato's reputation had, by design, nothing written down. In late 1925 — 1926, according to English Wikipedia's article on one of its own founders — he joined Nicolae Tonitza, Ștefan Dimitrescu and the sculptor Oscar Han to form Grupul celor patru, the Group of Four. What held it together was friendship and a shared instinct for colour harmony, not a manifesto or a shared style; the four painters and one sculptor went on painting differently from each other for as long as the group lasted. They showed together seven times between 1925 and 1934. Dimitrescu's death in 1933 ended it; the group held its final exhibition, without him, in March 1934.

sections.heading: A Museum Job That Rewired the Painting
sections.body: In 1917 Șirato was made custodian of the National Museum of Folk Art. Daily, close contact with peasant textiles and traditional pattern-work is credited with pulling his painting away from pure optical colour-division toward compositions built more from flat, constructed pattern and light. His landscapes drifted south and east with him, toward Balcic, Techirghiol and Mangalia on the Black Sea coast — then Romanian territory — subjects that almost every notable Romanian painter of his generation painted too, in a loose, retrospectively named grouping now called the Balcic school.

sections.heading: A Poet Bound a Book Around Him, and This Lake Still Has No Date
sections.body:
Tudor Arghezi, Romania's most consequential twentieth-century poet, thought enough of Șirato to publish a 1944 album on him bound with two original lithographs, and wrote that Șirato was a painter who kept thinking in colour after the brush left the canvas — that his paintings went on working past their own edges. Șirato taught at the Academy of Fine Arts in Bucharest from the early 1930s, won the National Prize for Painting in 1946, and held a final, well-received solo show in 1947 before he died in Bucharest in August 1953. A retrospective followed in Herăstrău Park in 1956.

Of this particular canvas, *Houses on the Shore of Lake Cernica*, no source gives a date, a medium or an exhibition history. It survives as one entry in a shoreline genre he returned to for decades, filed by WikiArt simply under Impressionism — a label the argument over what nationality painted it never quite gets around to unsettling.
